bills.title: Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026

bills.summary: This act reduces taxes, increases spending for various federal programs, and addresses agencies throughout the federal government as a reconciliation bill.
bills.brief: The bill provides tax cuts, modifies federal spending on agriculture, energy, and conservation, and adjusts immigration fees.
top_lines: Increases LIP payment rate to 100% for losses due to predation (from 75%).
Reduces cap on earnings transferred from Federal Reserve Board to CFPB from 12% to 6.5%.
Modifies Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act of 2006 to raise cap on distribution of OCS revenues to oil and gas producing Gulf states from $500 million to $650 million per year for FY2025-FY34.
bills.likelihoodReason: The bill has already become Public Law No: 119-21, indicating it was enacted. The sponsor is a Republican from Texas with zero cosponsors, but the reconciliation process and the fact that it became law suggest broad support or procedural necessity.

sections.label: Title I — COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE, NUTRITION, AND FORESTRY

items.main: Increases the payment rate under the Livestock Indemnity Program (LIP) to 100% for losses due to predation.
items.detail: Modifies the LIP payment rate for predation losses from 75% to 100%. The text cuts off mid-sentence regarding 'attacks by animals reintroduced'.

items.main: Reduces the cap on the percentage of combined earnings transferred from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).
items.detail: Changes the cap on earnings transferred from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve to the CFPB from 12% to 6.5%. The text cuts off before completing the provision.

items.main: Reduces restrictions on onshore development of oil and gas on federal lands by decreasing minimum royalty rates, reinstating noncompetitive leasing, directing Interior to resume quarterly lease sales in specified states, and approving applications allowing commingling of production from two or more sources before royalty payment measurement.
items.detail: Modifies existing restrictions on federal land oil and gas development. No new programs created; existing leasing practices modified (noncompetitive leasing reinstated).

sections.label: Title II — TAX POLICY AND REVENUE

items.main: Increases the percentage rate to 50% (from 25%) at which the alternative minimum tax exemption amount is phased out for individuals whose taxable income exceeds such threshold amount.
items.detail: The alternative minimum taxable income threshold amounts are $626,350 or $1,252,700 for joint filers for 2025, as adjusted annually for inflation beginning in 2026. Applies to individuals filing joint returns or married individuals filing separately.

items.main: Makes permanent the limit on the itemized tax deduction for home mortgage interest enacted in 2017 by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.
items.detail: Allows certain mortgage insurance premiums to be included in the itemized tax deduction for home mortgage interest. The limit is $750,000; $375,000 for married individuals filing separately.

items.main: Makes permanent and increases the tax deduction for charitable contributions made by individuals who do not itemize their federal income tax deductions.
items.detail: Increases the deduction amount to $1,000 for single filers (from $300) and $2,000 for joint filers (from $600 for joint filers). Makes it permanent.

items.main: Establishes a fee of at least $100 for applications for asylum.
items.detail: Applies to applicants for asylum. Provides exceptions on a case-by-case basis for the fee established in Sec. 100004 (e.g., life-threatening medical emergency).

items.main: Establishes a fee of at least $550 for asylees, parolees, or individuals granted temporary protected status who are applying for initial employment authorization.
items.detail: Applies to asylees, parolees, or individuals granted temporary protected status applying for initial employment authorization. Provides exceptions on a case-by-case basis for the fee established in Sec. 100004 (e.g., life-threatening medical emergency).

items.main: Eliminates the exemption from certain duties, fees, and processes for imports of up to $800 (commonly referred to as the de minimis exemption), effective July 1, 2027.
items.detail: Establishes a civil penalty for using such exemption in a manner that violates U.S. customs laws. Penalty: up to $5,000 for the first violation and up to $10,000 for subsequent violations.

bills.summary: The HEATS Act waives federal drilling permit requirements for geothermal exploration and production on non-federal lands if the U.S. owns less than 50% of the subsurface estate and a state permit is submitted.
bills.brief: This bill exempts certain geothermal activities from federal permitting, environmental review, and historic preservation requirements.
top_lines: Waives Federal drilling permit requirement for qualifying geothermal activities on non-Federal surface estate
Exempts qualifying activities from NEPA section 102(2)(C) and Endangered Species Act section 7
U.S. ownership interest must be less than 50 percent of the subsurface geothermal estate
bills.likelihoodReason: The bill has only 2 cosponsors in the House, which is a very low number for passage. The sponsor is a Republican from California (R-CA), and the latest action shows a motion to reconsider was laid on the table without objection, indicating limited debate or support. The provision waives federal permitting requirements, which may attract opposition from environmental groups or representatives concerned about regulatory oversight.

sections.label: Title I — Harnessing Energy At Thermal Sources Act

items.main: Waives the requirement for a Federal drilling permit for geothermal exploration and production activities conducted on a non-Federal surface estate, provided that (1) the United States holds an ownership interest of less than 50 percent of the subsurface geothermal estate to be accessed by the proposed action; and (2) the operator submits to the Secretary a State permit to conduct geothermal exploration and production activities on the non-Federal surface estate.
items.detail: The bill amends the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970 by adding Section 30. It exempts such activity from NEPA section 102(2)(C) and Endangered Species Act section 7, subject to conditions. The Secretary may conduct onsite reviews and inspections for accountability, measurement, reporting, and royalty payment.

underreported.section: Section 30 of the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970
underreported.summary: The provision states that royalties due to the United States under this Act from production of electricity using geothermal resources (other than direct use) or byproducts are not affected.
underreported.why_unreported: Royalty obligations remain intact despite the waiver of drilling permits, which may be overlooked in summaries focusing solely on permitting relief.

gaps: The bill does not address potential impacts on tribal lands or resources managed in trust for Indian Tribes beyond simply excluding them from the waiver.
The bill does not specify how state permits are evaluated to ensure they meet environmental standards comparable to federal requirements.

added: New Section 30 in the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970
modified: Geothermal Steam Act of 1970 — adds waiver for Federal drilling permit requirement for certain geothermal activities
removed: Requirement for a Federal drilling permit for qualifying geothermal activities on non-Federal surface estate

bills.title: HEATS Act
Main Street Capital Access Act
bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed committee 26-16 with 33 cosponsors. Its eight titles span genuinely bipartisan community bank relief to politically charged provisions — reputational risk elimination and antitrust exemptions for mergers — that will complicate Senate passage. Community bank capital relief and exam reform have Senate allies, but the Operation Choke Point language and NGFS reporting requirements will provoke Democratic opposition.

items.main: Provides a 3-year phase-in of capital requirements for newly chartered banks and lowers the leverage ratio to 7.5% for new rural banks.
items.detail: De novo bank formation has nearly stopped — fewer than 5 new charters per year since 2010 versus 150+ annually before the financial crisis. The phase-in gives new banks runway to build capital without immediate full compliance. The rural bank leverage ratio reduction is specifically calibrated for communities with fewer than 50,000 residents.

comments.text: R-Financial Services: Regulatory barriers are strangling new bank formation in underserved markets.
D-Financial Services: Supportive of new charters but concerned lighter capital rules apply during the riskiest early years.

items.main: Extends the CDFI Bond Guarantee Program through 2028 and raises the minimum bond guarantee floor to $25 million.
items.detail: CDFIs serve low-income and rural markets that conventional banks have exited. The bond guarantee provides long-term capital at lower cost. The $25M minimum may exclude the smallest CDFIs that need it most.

comments.text: D: CDFI expansion is the most broadly supported provision in the bill across both parties.
CDFI Coalition: The $25M minimum is too high for the smallest community lenders we represent.

items.main: Raises dozens of Dodd-Frank asset thresholds to reflect GDP growth since 2010, with automatic future adjustments every 5 years tied to GDP.
items.detail: The Community Bank Leverage Ratio threshold rises from $10B to $15B. Enhanced prudential standards threshold rises from $250B to $370B. Small Bank Holding Company threshold rises to $6B. Every threshold in the bill auto-adjusts to future GDP growth — structurally removing Congress from future threshold decisions.

comments.text: R: Dollar amounts set in 2010 represent much stricter standards in real terms today; this corrects inflation drift.
D: These thresholds exist because of 2008. Inflation adjustment is a pretext for deregulation.

items.main: Raises the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act small-institution exemption from $30 million to $160 million in assets.
items.detail: Banks under $160M will no longer report mortgage data broken down by race, income, and geography — the primary dataset used to identify lending discrimination. The change exempts the vast majority of community banks from fair lending data collection.

comments.text: R: Small banks face crushing compliance costs for data collection with minimal regulatory value.
D-Fair Housing: Eliminating HMDA data for community banks removes visibility into redlining at the local level where it most commonly occurs.

items.main: Raises Community Reinvestment Act small-bank threshold from $250 million to $800 million, exempting far more banks from full CRA exams.
items.detail: CRA requires banks to reinvest in communities where they take deposits, particularly low-income neighborhoods. Banks under $800M now qualify for a streamlined exam. At $800M, this captures the vast majority of U.S. community banks.

comments.text: R: CRA compliance is a massive burden for small banks already deeply invested in their local communities.
National Community Reinvestment Coalition: The threshold increase will reduce accountability for banks serving low-income neighborhoods.

items.main: Creates an Office of Independent Examination Review — a new presidential-appointee body that can overrule bank examiner decisions using de novo (fresh) review.
items.detail: Banks disputing CAMELS ratings or any material supervisory determination can appeal to this Office, which reviews without deferring to examiners and can hold formal hearings with testimony under oath. Its decisions bind the regulatory agency. Banks may also elect to take enforcement actions to federal district court instead of administrative proceedings.

comments.text: R: Examiners have operated with unchecked subjective judgment for decades; independent review creates necessary accountability.
D: This politicizes bank supervision by inserting presidential appointees into technical regulatory determinations.

items.main: Bans all federal banking agencies from ever considering reputational risk in supervision, explicitly referencing Operation Choke Point.
items.detail: The prohibition is absolute: no guidance, exam criteria, or enforcement action may reference reputational risk — the mechanism regulators used to pressure banks to exit clients in firearms, payday lending, and similar legal industries. The explicit Operation Choke Point reference signals this is a politically motivated provision targeting perceived weaponization of banking supervision.

comments.text: R: Operation Choke Point was unlawful weaponization of banking regulation against legal businesses.
D: Reputational risk is a legitimate safety and soundness concern; banks serving fraudulent businesses face real losses.

items.main: Exempts all bank mergers resulting in institutions under $10 billion in assets from antitrust competition review.
items.detail: Current law requires all bank mergers to be evaluated for anticompetitive effects. Section 601 eliminates this review for mergers resulting in banks under $10B. Since the vast majority of U.S. banks fall below this threshold, this effectively removes antitrust oversight from most bank merger activity.

comments.text: R: Community bank mergers do not create systemic competition concerns; regulators spend resources on the wrong problems.
D: Banking deserts have grown as local banks consolidate. Competition review exists precisely to catch local monopolies.

items.main: Imposes a 120-day hard deadline on all merger approvals; applications are deemed approved automatically if regulators miss the deadline.
items.detail: Deemed-approved provisions transfer power from regulators to applicants. If an agency cannot complete its review — due to complexity, resource constraints, or significant public comment volume — the merger proceeds automatically. Particularly significant for mergers that attract community opposition.

comments.text: R: Regulators use delay as de facto denial; hard deadlines create accountability.
D: Community groups and regulators need adequate time; automatic approvals bypass public input entirely.

underreported.section: Section 404 — Mandatory Reporting on NGFS Interactions
underreported.summary: Forces the Federal Reserve, OCC, and FDIC to publicly report annually on every interaction with the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) — a global climate risk supervisory body. The NGFS is explicitly named in the bill.
underreported.why_unreported: Framed as a transparency measure, this is a direct mechanism to chill the Fed's participation in climate-related financial risk supervision without formally prohibiting it. By requiring public disclosure of every NGFS interaction, the bill creates political exposure for climate-focused supervisory work. Coverage has focused entirely on capital and exam provisions; this climate surveillance mechanism has received almost no attention.

underreported.section: Section 601 — Antitrust Exemption Creates Automatic Merger Approval Risk
underreported.summary: The 120-day deemed-approved provision combined with the antitrust exemption means a community bank merger can close with no competition review and no public input if regulators are overwhelmed or slow — a scenario made more likely in a banking crisis when merger volume spikes.
underreported.why_unreported: The deemed-approved mechanism appears in a section headlined as 'clarity and predictability.' The risk that mergers auto-approve during periods of banking stress — exactly when review is most needed — has not featured in any coverage of the bill.

underreported.section: Section 701 — FDIC Can Pay More to Avoid GSIB Acquisitions of Failed Banks
underreported.summary: Allows the FDIC to pay more from the Deposit Insurance Fund specifically to prevent a failing bank from being acquired by a global systemically important bank, even when the GSIB offers the cheapest resolution. A rare anti-concentration provision inside a predominantly deregulatory bill.
underreported.why_unreported: This provision directly addresses the 2023 SVB/First Republic controversy where JPMorgan expanded through FDIC-assisted acquisitions. It has bipartisan support but has been entirely absent from coverage because it contradicts the bill's overall deregulatory frame and requires understanding the GSIB framework.

criticisms.why: HMDA threshold rollback removes fair lending data for most community banks; reputational risk prohibition will give banks cover to deny services to cannabis businesses in legal states; antitrust exemption for sub-$10B mergers will accelerate rural banking consolidation.

Reduced examination frequency combined with HMDA data rollback removes the two primary tools used to identify predatory lending at small institutions — the least visible and most likely sites of consumer harm.

The NGFS reporting requirement is an attempt to expose and suppress climate risk supervision within the Fed without directly prohibiting it — a backdoor attack on financial climate policy disguised as transparency.

gaps: No provision addressing rent-a-bank schemes where fintechs partner with small state-chartered banks to issue loans above state usury caps — a significant consumer harm growing rapidly and directly related to the fintech partnerships studied in Title VIII.
Silent on overdraft fee practices at community banks and credit unions despite providing those same institutions with broad regulatory relief throughout the bill.

Title VIII studies on bank-fintech partnerships produce reports but no regulatory framework — a missed opportunity given that unregulated fintech partnerships are generating the next generation of consumer harms.

No provision addressing the banking access gap for legal cannabis businesses in states where it is permitted — ironic given that the reputational risk prohibition was specifically intended to help those businesses.

bills.title: Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, FY2027
bills.likelihoodReason: Military construction and VA appropriations bills are among the least controversial annual spending bills and typically pass with bipartisan support. The House Appropriations Committee reported it, placing it on the Union Calendar. A continuing resolution fight or broader budget standoff remains the primary risk to passage this fiscal year.

items.main: Funds construction and renovation of military bases, barracks, and training facilities across all service branches.
items.detail: Covers family housing, medical facilities, and critical infrastructure upgrades at installations worldwide. Includes funding for installations in the Indo-Pacific region as part of the ongoing strategic rebalance toward countering China.

comments.text: R-Leadership: Essential for military readiness and force projection.
D-Armed Services: Supports the funding levels but wants more focus on domestic base communities.

items.main: Allocates funds for PFAS contamination cleanup at military installations.
items.detail: Addresses firefighting foam (AFFF) contamination that has polluted groundwater near dozens of bases. The cleanup mandate has bipartisan backing but the funding level is disputed — environmental groups argue it is insufficient.

comments.text: D-Environment: The allocation falls well short of EPA estimates for full remediation.
Veterans advocates: Cleanup directly tied to service-member health claims.

items.main: Funds VA hospitals, clinics, and mental health programs serving over 9 million enrolled veterans.
items.detail: Covers staffing, medical equipment, telehealth expansion, and the MISSION Act community care program which allows veterans to seek care outside the VA system. Community care has grown rapidly and now consumes a significant share of the VHA budget.

comments.text: R-VA Committee: Supports expansion of community care as a market-based solution.
D-VA Committee: Concerned that community care funding draws resources from VA facility investment.

items.main: Maintains funding for the PACT Act toxic exposure claims backlog processing.
items.detail: The PACT Act (2022) expanded eligibility for veterans exposed to burn pits, Agent Orange, and radiation. The VA faces a claims backlog running into the hundreds of thousands. This bill continues emergency processing staffing, though veterans groups say the pace remains too slow.

comments.text: Veterans of Foreign Wars: Processing times have improved but remain unacceptable for dying veterans.

items.main: Funds disability compensation, pension, education (GI Bill), and vocational rehabilitation benefits.
items.detail: The largest single line item in the bill. Disability compensation alone accounts for the majority of VBA spending. Post-PACT Act, benefit outlays have increased significantly and the appropriation reflects continued growth in the eligible veteran population.

comments.text: R-Budget: Growth in mandatory-like spending within discretionary appropriations is structurally difficult.

underreported.summary: Expands third-party administrator authority to deny VA community care referrals, effectively giving private contractors power to gatekeep which veterans can seek outside care.
underreported.why_unreported: Buried in administrative contract language; framed as 'cost management' but functionally restricts a benefit veterans assumed was guaranteed by the MISSION Act.

underreported.section: Section 412 — Relocation of Arlington Annex Operations
underreported.summary: Quietly relocates several American Battle Monuments Commission administrative functions, reducing the civilian workforce at a historic site with no public debate.
underreported.why_unreported: Grouped under 'related agencies' which receive almost no media coverage in appropriations reporting.

criticisms.why: Mental health staffing ratios at VA facilities are inadequate; the bill does not meet the 1:1500 psychiatrist-to-veteran ratio recommended by the VA's own inspector general.
Total VA discretionary spending has grown 75% since 2019; some members argue structural reform is needed before further increases.

gaps: No provision addressing the ~300,000 veteran homelessness cases despite VA housing programs being funded separately through HUD.
Silent on VA electronic health record modernization project, which has been repeatedly delayed and over-budget.
No accountability mechanism for community care contractors who deny referrals.

featured_quotes.text: The mental health clinic funding is the largest single VA expansion since the PACT Act.

featured_quotes.name: Rep. Chip Roy
featured_quotes.text: We are still spending more on consultants than on actual concrete. I will vote no.

bills.brief: Must-pass appropriations bill with broad bipartisan support — the primary risk is a wider budget standoff, not the bill itself.

Adds $890M for veteran mental health clinics in 12 underserved counties
Section 223 quietly strips the standing GAO audit trigger on $1.2B in unobligated DoD funds

modified: Cemetery expansion funding redirected from East Coast to Mountain West

bills.title: Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026
bills.likelihoodReason: Farm bills historically pass but this one is unusually contentious. The Agriculture Committee voted 34-17 to report it — a wider party-line margin than typical farm bills. Democratic opposition to SNAP modifications and conservative pressure to cut more deeply both make floor passage and Senate negotiation difficult. A short-term extension remains likely if the bill stalls.

items.main: Updates reference prices for corn, wheat, soybeans, cotton, and other covered commodities triggering government support payments.
items.detail: The Agriculture Risk Coverage (ARC) and Price Loss Coverage (PLC) programs pay farmers when market prices fall below statutory reference levels. This bill raises those reference prices for the first time since 2014, effectively guaranteeing higher government payments regardless of market conditions.

comments.text: R-Agriculture: Reference prices haven't kept up with input cost inflation; farmers need certainty.
D-Agriculture: Raises support for large commodity operations while rural communities see no benefit.

items.main: Modifies Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program work requirements, expanding mandatory employment and training participation.
items.detail: Raises the age threshold for able-bodied adults without dependents subject to work requirements from 49 to 54. Also limits state waiver authority that previously exempted high-unemployment areas. Congressional Budget Office estimates this reduces SNAP enrollment by approximately 2-3 million participants over 10 years.

comments.text: R-Leadership: Encourages workforce participation and targets benefits to those who cannot work.
D-Nutrition: Cuts food assistance to elderly and rural Americans who face genuine barriers to employment.

items.main: Restricts purchase of U.S. agricultural land by entities linked to China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.
items.detail: Requires divestiture of existing holdings above a threshold acreage within five years. Creates a new USDA registry of foreign-owned farmland with mandatory annual reporting. Critics note that enforcement mechanisms are vague and penalties are modest.

comments.text: R-National Security: Foreign adversary ownership near military installations is a direct security threat.
D-Agriculture: Support the concept but the enforcement structure lacks teeth.

items.main: Reauthorizes Conservation Reserve Program (CRP) with a slightly increased acreage cap, and modifies Environmental Quality Incentives Program (EQIP) payment limits.
items.detail: CRP pays farmers to take environmentally sensitive land out of production. The new cap allows enrollment of up to 27 million acres, up from 25 million. However, climate-focused conservation funding enacted in the Inflation Reduction Act is redirected into baseline programs, effectively reducing climate-specific spending.

comments.text: D-Environment: Hollows out the IRA's climate conservation investments without saying so explicitly.
R-Agriculture: Returns conservation funding to farmers rather than climate ideology.

underreported.summary: Quietly redirects approximately $18 billion in Inflation Reduction Act climate conservation funding into general EQIP and RCPP accounts, stripping the climate-specific use requirements without explicitly repealing the IRA provision.
underreported.why_unreported: Reported as a 'consolidation' of conservation programs; the IRA climate funding redirection has received almost no coverage outside of agricultural trade press despite being one of the largest effective climate policy reversals in the bill.

underreported.summary: Narrows the definition of 'bioengineered food' subject to USDA disclosure requirements, exempting highly refined products where engineered DNA is no longer detectable — effectively gutting GMO labeling for most processed foods.
underreported.why_unreported: Framed as 'technical alignment' with existing USDA standards; the practical effect is that most grocery store products that currently carry bioengineered disclosures would no longer be required to.

underreported.summary: Changes eligibility criteria for USDA rural development hospital grants in a way that excludes recently reclassified rural communities that gained suburban designation in the 2020 census.
underreported.why_unreported: Buried in the rural development title; affects dozens of small hospital systems that gained population but remain economically rural in character.

criticisms.why: SNAP modifications effectively cut food assistance to 2-3 million low-income Americans, targeting a program that is 80% of the farm bill's total cost but benefits the most vulnerable.
IRA conservation climate funding is redirected without debate, representing one of the largest rollbacks of climate investment since the IRA's passage.
Commodity reference price increases lock in higher subsidy payments regardless of market conditions, removing market discipline from agriculture policy.

gaps: No provision addressing consolidation in the meatpacking industry, where four companies control over 80% of beef processing.
Silent on crop insurance subsidies for mega-farms — the top 10% of recipients receive over 50% of payments but payment limits are unchanged.
No mechanism to address the mental health crisis in farm communities despite record farm debt and suicide rates.

featured_quotes.name: Sen. Cory Booker
featured_quotes.text: We are using a farm bill to override state environmental law. That is not what this committee was built for.

featured_quotes.name: Rep. Glenn Thompson
featured_quotes.text: American farmers cannot operate under fifty different rulebooks. This is a unity bill.

bills.brief: Contentious SNAP modifications and IRA funding redirection make Senate passage uncertain despite the inevitable farm bill tradition.
top_lines: Reauthorizes $770B in farm and nutrition programs through FY2031
Expands SNAP work requirements — CBO estimates 2-3 million lose eligibility
Redirects $18B in Inflation Reduction Act climate conservation funding to general agricultural programs

added: $8B rural broadband expansion through USDA ReConnect
modified: SNAP work requirement expanded to ages 18–64 (was 18–54)
Crop insurance subsidy floor raised from 62% to 70%
removed: Drops Conservation Reserve Program acreage cap increase

bills.summary: Reauthorizes USDA programs through 2030. Restructures SNAP work requirements, expands crop insurance, adds rural broadband.
